titleStmt.title: Towards Automatic Synthesis of QoS Preserving Implementations from Object-Oriented Design Models

analytic.title: Towards Automatic Synthesis of QoS Preserving Implementations from Object-Oriented Design Models

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The translation of object-oriented design models into implementation requires a number of decisions to be made before code can be generated. Besides choosing the target platform, these decisions also include strategies for multi-tasking and scheduling, the selection of scheduling attributes, etc. Such decisions clearly impact the QoS properties of the implemented system. In this paper, we address the problem of synthesizing QoS preserving implementations from object-oriented design models. Based on our recent research experience in applying fixed priority schedulability analysis techniques to real-time object-oriented designs, we present some of the obstacles in automating this process. We also present a brief overview of our research results in addressing this problem.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The design of real-time systems poses unique challenges since not only the functional requirements must be met, but also the system must be designed to predictably meet its non-functional, or quality of service (QoS) requirements. Such QoS requirements take various forms, and may include requirements on timeliness, reliability, availability, and security. In particular, timeliness requirements form a central and core aspect of real-time systems. While the notion of timeliness encompasses a broad variety of timing requirements, the notion of schedulability is generally associated with the ability of a system to meet its deadlines.

Despite the wide-spread prevalence of real-time systems in industry, the design of such systems include many ad-hoc steps, albeit often guided by engineering intuition. While these ad-hoc procedures may be acceptable for systems with limited functional complexity, or with lax timing constraints, the increasing complexity of such systems is clearly exposing the limits of such methods. Fortunately, a number of advances have taken place in the last two decades or so, and these advances are now reflecting in a new generation of design tools for real-time systems design. Notable among these advances are: (1) real-time schedulability analysis techniques to predict whether a given system will meet its deadlines or not, and (2) object-oriented modeling languages and design methods to address the increasing functional complexity of such systems.

Schedulability analysis techniques allow a developer to predict the worst-case response times, and hence the schedulability (i.e., whether the system will meet its deadlines) of a system. Many of the techniques are based on preemptive priority scheduling of tasks. One of the most mature of these techniques is for fixed-priority preemptive scheduling (e.g., [16,15,14,9,24]), which often goes by the name of "rate-monotonic analysis" [13]. Similar techniques have been developed for earliest deadline scheduling, which can potentially offer higher schedulable utilizations, but may incur higher overheads. Some newer approaches have also started addressing stochastic real-time properties [10,1,23].

In parallel to the efforts on real-time schedulability analysis techniques, object-oriented modeling and design has gained popularity in the real-time circles to combat the increasing functional complexity of such systems. There are a number of efforts to re-orient object-oriented technologies towards the modeling and design of real-time systems. Object oriented analysis and design models include various modeling abstractions and concepts such as active objects and finite state machines to model system structure and behavior. By using visual modeling of abstractions that are closer to the problem space, object-oriented modeling and design facilitates the design process and promotes a better understanding of the design. Furthermore, such models also facilitate various forms of analysis and simulation to help in the design process.

There have been a few attempts to integrate the advances in schedulability analysis and object-oriented design methods (e.g., [8,3,5,6]), but not without problems. The main source of these problems comes from the mapping an object design to a multi-tasking implementation. In our own work [17,21], we have addressed the problem of integrating schedulability analysis techniques with an industrial strength object-oriented design tool (ObjecTime Developer), and found a number of problems in doing so.

In this paper, we present our perspective on how schedulability analysis techniques can be integrated into design tools based on object-oriented design methods. Our approach is to make this integration seamless, and use automation (as far as feasible) to allow a developer to focus on solving the design problems at high levels of abstractions, provided by object-oriented design methods. The system should then automatically synthesize implementations from the designs (and in the process making low-level implementation decisions) that preserve not only the functional integrity of the design models, but also ensure that the timing requirements will be met in the implemented system.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we investigate the state of the art in automation support for real-time system development. Then, in Section 3, we reflect upon the obstacles to automatic synthesis. In Section 4, we outline our approach and current results towards addressing this problem. Finally, we present some concluding remarks.

div.head: Automation Support for Real-Time System Development
div.p: With the maturity of technology in object-oriented design, and real-time schedulability analysis techniques, a number of tools are emerging that automate parts of the development process. Perhaps, one of the most significant developments on this front is the support for automatic code generation from design models. With such automatic code-generation, the benefits of model based design extend through the product's life-cycle. Automatic code-generation is especially critical with an iterative and incremental development style. In the absence of codegeneration, developers will often bypass the models and directly modify the code when pressed for time. Thus, models get out of sync with the code, and become less relevant. When code generation is supported, the models retain their usefulness, and the design models become the implementation [4,22].

While code-generation from object-oriented models has received little attention in the research literature, it has been successfully achieved in a few commercial tools. Most notable among these are the ObjecTime Developer from Ob-jecTime, Rational Rose Real-Time from Rational and Ob-jecTime, and Rhapsody from i-Logix. 1 The basic approach followed in these tools consists of: (1) restricting the object models to an executable subset; (2) extending the modeling language with a detail level programming language to specify detailed structure and behavior (e.g., description of data classes, code segments associated with finite state machine transitions, etc.); and (3) providing a real-time execution framework that facilitates code generation, and provides an API to be used in the application code segments.

Figure 1 shows a typical (albeit simplified) development cycle that one might follow with such design tools. A design tool is used to incrementally model the application objects (and classes), the structural relationships between them, and behavioral specifications of the classes. The behavioral specifications may include code segments in a target programming language. The tools also provide support for model simulation to test for functional correctness. Once there is a stable design model, the developer can generate code for a desired target platform. However, before code can be generated, certain implementation decisions must be made. Such implementation decisions include:

(1) choice of target environment (operating system, compiler, etc.), (2) allocation of objects to the nodes in a multiprocessor/distributed system, (3) choosing operating system threads, assigning them attributes (e.g., priority) and mapping objects to threads. Once an implementation model is designed, then the code generator can be used to build the target executable(s), which can then be downloaded on the target platform for target testing.

Current generation of design tools lack support for quality-of-service assessment and prediction, and developers must use separate tools (or worse-still, use targettesting) to make such assessments. A few commercial tools (e.g., TimeWiz2 , and RapidRMA3 ) are available to perform schedulablity analysis, but the lack of integration between such tools and the design tools requires that a developer must manually derive performance analysis models from their design models before such tools can be used. Any given design model presents a number of implementation choices. In the absence of a clear understanding on what implementation decisions are "correct," (in the sense of preserving QoS requirements) a developer may have to make these decisions in a somewhat loose and ad-hoc manner, and hope that the requirements will be met. This can easily result in "lengthy" fine-tuning cycles to iterate to a correct implementation. Furthermore, this process must be repeated frequently in evolving systems, whenever new functionality is added, or when timing requirements change.

One of the benefits of object-oriented design methods is that they offer higher level of abstractions (as compared to programming languages and operating systems), and this helps developers handle the increasing complexity of realtime software. At the same time, due to this disconnect between design models and their implementation, multiple implementation alternatives are available to map the design to an implementation. As systems become more complex, the mapping of designs to a feasible implementation becomes a challenging problem. It also affords possibilities for automation. We believe that automation support for implementation synthesis is an important ingredient in the efficient development of real-time software. Such automation support should guide a developer to quickly correct implementation choices.

div.head: Obstacles to Automatic Implementation Synthesis
div.p: There are a number of obstacles to overcome in order to support automatic synthesis of implementation. We gained some insights into this problem through our work on applying real-time scheduling theory to design models generated with ObjecTime Developer toolset. The following sub-sections highlight some of the obstacles that we have encountered in our own efforts.

div.head: End-to-End Behavior Modeling in OO-Design Models
div.p: Many QoS properties, including real-time properties of rate and latencies are most naturally specified on end-to-end behaviors from system inputs to system outputs. Furthermore, detailed end-to-end behavior modeling is critical for the derivation of performance models for predicting realtime performance. Unfortunately, we find that while objectoriented methods and modeling languages have evolved to use powerful modeling notations for modeling structures (e.g., classes and their associations, objects and their associations, layering, hierarchical decomposition, etc.), and object behavior (state diagrams), they are quite weak in endto-end behavior modeling.

Typically, sequence diagrams or message sequence charts are used for end-to-end behavior modeling. While these notations are useful in showing inter-object communications and sequencing of such message flows, they have several problems. First, the semantics of sequence diagrams are not very clear. Second, sequence diagrams are only intended to show "typical" scenarios, and unlike state diagrams do not capture a full specification end-to-end behaviors. Also, sequence diagrams are weak at showing concurrency (arising from asynchronous message flows) within a scenario, and also in showing conditional behaviors. For all of these reasons, it is difficult to derive accurate performance models from the design models.

div.head: Limitations of QoS Prediction Techniques
div.p: A second obstacle to automatic synthesis is the limitation of the QoS prediction techniques. Even for real-time schedulability analysis, where the techniques are most welldeveloped, there is a disconnect between the implementation models used in the theory, and the implementation models used in practice with object-oriented designs. For example, most real-time schedulability analysis techniques are based on preemptive tasking models, where each task performs a single activity, and participates in only one timing constraint. Thus a task's scheduling attributes (e.g., priority) are automatically based on its timing constraint. The implementation models of object-oriented designs often use event-driven implementation architectures, where a single task may be used to process events from multiple sources and with different timing constraints, with the action to be performed depending on the event, and the internal state of the system.

The limitations of QoS prediction techniques are greater when the worst-case assumptions are relaxed, and stochastic assumptions are used. Even though there have been a few recent papers addressing stochastic schedulability analysis (e.g., [11,10,1,23]), the techniques are still relatively immature. Moreover, the tasking models are more restrictive than the ones used for deterministic schedulability analysis. The use of these techniques with object-oriented design models would necessitate the development of approximate performance models. Much more research is needed to make effective use of such techniques into the objectoriented design process.

div.head: Integration of QoS Prediction and Design
div.p: Most work on real-time scheduling has concentrated on determining schedulability of an already designed system, where all design decisions have been made, and the problem is restricted to assessing the response times. This ignores the problem of making design (or implementation decisions) that achieve the desired QoS. In recent years, a few papers have addressed this issue. For example, Audsley [2] addresses the problem of assigning priorities to tasks such that the timing constraints are satisfied under fixed-priority preemptive scheduling. Allocation of tasks to processors is another well studied problem in research literature. In our previous work [7,18], we studied the problem of automatically deriving task attributes (e.g., periods and deadlines) from high level end-to-end constraints (e.g., min and max periods, end-to-end deadlines). In [10], we extended this approach to determine processor shares for tasks with stochastic throughput/latency requirements.

With object-oriented design models, there are even greater number of design/implementation decisions that must be made. One such decision is whether the implementation will use a single threaded or a multi-threaded implementation architecture. If a multi-threaded architecture is used then a mapping of the design elements to the multiple threads must be designed. Other decisions involve choosing a scheduling strategy and scheduling attributes. Typically there are two levels of scheduling: task level, and message/event level (within a single task). The number of such design decisions increase if one considers more QoS aspects. For example, if fault-tolerance is introduced, then one must choose between replication schemes (active or passive), number of replicas, etc. Similarly, when stochastic assumptions are used, one must also consider policies for overload detection and handling. Ultimately, all such design decisions impact QoS, and therefore there is a need to integrate QoS predictions for making these design decisions.

div.head: Workload Modeling
div.p: One of the assumptions used in all schedulability analysis techniques is that the workload is assumed to be known. Accurate workload modeling is necessary for the results of any QoS prediction to be valid. Workload modeling involves modeling of the rates of external events (or stimuli to the system), and the resource demands of the actions taken to handle the events. In many real-time systems, the rates of external events is controlled and known, due to periodic time-triggered sampling. Still, such polling is not always desirable for asynchronous events, and there is a need to model their arrival rates. A harder problem, perhaps, is the estimation of resource demands of actions. In a complex real-time system, deriving (or measuring) resource demands of these actions can easily be a daunting task.

div.head: Towards Automatic Implementation Synthesis
div.p: We are developing an approach geared towards automatic synthesis of implementations that predictably meet the QoS requirements of an application. Our initial efforts have focused on uniprocessor systems with hard real-time timing constraints. Therefore, our work has concentrated on integration of real-time schedulability analysis techniques with object-oriented design methods. Object-oriented design models may be implemented in a number of different ways. Here, we will concentrate on multi-tasking and scheduling issues only. Techniques to translate class and state diagrams into code can be found in [22,6].

div.head: Single Threaded Implementation Architecture
div.p: In implementing object-oriented design models, one of the first decisions to be made is whether the implementation will be single threaded, or multi-threaded. In a single threaded implementation, a single thread is implemented as an event handler. All events, whether external or internal, are placed on an event queue when they are generated. The thread executes an event loop, and in each loop removes an event and processes it to completion. This simple scheme is quite effective in many cases, and provides a very low overhead, non-preemptive multi-tasking strategy. In a single threaded implementation, the scheduling problem is reduced to the processing order of events queued in the event queue. A simple and effective strategy is to use (fixed) priorities for events, and to process events in priority order.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis and Implementation Synthesis
div.p: Schedulability analysis for single-threaded implementations can be carried out by a simple extension to the traditional fixed priority schedulability analysis techniques [19].

Here each event and the corresponding action to handle the event may be viewed as a task (for the purpose of analysis), and the scheduling is non-preemptive. For single threaded implementations, with fixed event priorities, the synthesis problem is reduced to determining optimal (or feasible) event priorities, and one could use the algorithm developed by Audsley [2] for that purpose. The synthesis problem can be easily extended to include assignments of periods and intermediate deadlines [18,7] as well.

The single threaded approach may not be appropriate when there are compute-intensive actions, as may happen with many signal processing applications. Since the scheduling of events is non-preemptive, a compute intensive action can easily cause missed deadlines due to priority inversion. In such cases, it may be necessary to use multithreaded implementation architectures. Multi-threaded architectures may also be necessary for multiprocessor and distributed systems (to exploit the parallelism) and when actions may block.

div.head: Multi-Threaded Implementation Architectures
div.p: In a multi-threaded implementation architecture there are multiple threads, with each thread implemented as an event handler, and executing an event-handling loop. Multithreaded architectures allow the possibility of preemption (even though processing of an event is non-preemptive within a thread, it can be preempted by another thread) in uniprocessor systems. In a multi-threaded implementation, there are two levels of scheduling. Within the context of a single thread, the processing of events is determined by the scheduling policy within the thread, and may be based on event priorities, as in single-threaded implementations. Across the whole system, the operating system schedules the threads. Thread scheduling in most real-time operating systems is based on thread priorities.

This two level scheduling must be carefully managed to meet the timing requirements of the system. Assuming that event priorities have been assigned, and that the objective is to process higher priority events first, then static thread priorities will, in general, lead to significant priority inversions. This is, because, a thread may be processing events of different priorities, and therefore, a single fixed thread priority cannot adequately represent all events that it may process. Therefore, as we argued in [17,21], a thread's priority should be dynamically managed to reflect the priority of the highest pending event in its event queue (and the current event being processed, if any). This can be done transparently by the run-time libraries of the real-time execution framework.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: When thread priorities are dynamically managed, as discussed above, then priority inversion (defined as the processing of a lower priority event, when a higher priority event is pending) is bounded. Schedulability analysis can then be applied by extending the fixed priority schedulability analysis techniques to account for the dynamic management of thread priorities and the two level scheduling. While the schedulability analysis uses the same basic techniques (critical instant and busy period analysis), it differs in the details to account for the peculiarities of the computational model. The details of schedulability analysis can be found in [19,12].

div.head: Implementation Synthesis
div.p: In a multi-threaded implementation architecture, as described above, a number of implementation decisions must be made. First, as in the single-threaded architecture, we must assign priorities to events. Then, a mapping of events to threads must be generated. While this mapping can, in general, be arbitrary, there are implications on overheads and timing properties. We discuss a few possible strategies. In all cases, the synthesis problem requires deciding the number of threads, and a mapping of the events to the threads.

One strategy is to map objects to threads. Thus, all events that are destined to a particular object will be processed within the same thread. This is the strategy used in ObjecTime Developer, Rhapsody, and Rational Rose Real-Time. One clear advantage of this strategy is that object consistency is obtained for free, since access to an object is restricted to one thread. A disadvantage of this strategy is the overhead that comes with dynamically managed thread priorities (to bound priority inversion).

An alternate strategy is to assign threads to timing constraints, i.e., create a separate thread for each timing constraint. With this approach, there is no need to dynamically manage thread priorities, but it may result in a large number of threads, and the strategy may not scale to complex systems. Another drawback is that multiple threads may access an object, and therefore, it may be necessary to use locks with objects to ensure object consistency.

Another strategy is to create ¡ threads, one for each priority level, and assign all events at priority ¢ to the thread with priority ¢ . It has the same advantages as associating threads with timing constraints, but it scales up better for large complex systems.

The implementation synthesis problem then is to choose among these (and other) possibilities for mapping events to threads. This process can be automated by using a search algorithm that searches over the range of "valid" mappings of events to threads to find a feasible mapping, i.e., one that meets the timing requirements of the system. In our initial work [20], we have developed an algorithm that attempts to minimize the number of threads in the system. The search algorithm uses schedulability analysis in its inner-loop to search through the range of valid mappings.

div.head: Prototype Implementation
div.p: In order to test and validate our ideas, we have been developing a prototype toolset. We have already built a schedulability analysis tool, and are in the process of building search algorithms for implementation algorithms. We are also building a code-generator for a restricted subset of Unified Modeling Language so that the synthesized implementation models can be used to generate code. We expect that the toolset implementation will serve as a testbed for evaluating different implementation strategies, their impact on QoS, and incorporating them into implementation synthesis. In the longer run, we also expect to integrate the algorithms developed in the project with commercial tools (Rational Rose Real-Time, and TimeWiz), and to apply the ideas to applications developed using these tools.

div.head: Concluding Remarks
div.p: We have presented the problem of automatic synthesis of implementations from real-time object-oriented design models and outlined some of the obstacles in achieving that. We have also presented an overview of our research efforts in making this a reality for uniprocessor systems with hard real-time constraints. Our effort, so far, has focused on schedulability analysis of such systems, and in using the results to synthesize the implementation models.

The automatic synthesis process releases a designer from the burden of selecting various implementation artifacts (priorities of events and mapping of events to threads), in much the same way automatic code generation releases a designer from the burden of deciding how to implement the modeling abstractions. We believe that automating the synthesis process will greatly improve the state of the art in real-time software development.

We note that our work is still in preliminary stages, and much more work needs to be done. The synthesis problem gets harder as one goes from uniprocessor to multiprocessor and distributed systems. Likewise, the relaxation of hardness on timing constraints adds a new level of difficulty in both accurate QoS prediction and using that to synthesize implementations. Finally, other QoS dimensions add another level of complexity to the problem.
